title: Proposed trust tax change would make 'collateral damage' to small, family businesses, COSBOA says
transcript:
Speaker 0: The government hopes its proposed 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts and capital gains carve out for startups will pass parliament in this sitting fortnight.
Speaker 0: Skye Capucho is the CEO
Speaker 0: of the Council of Small Business Organizations
Speaker 0: Australia,
Speaker 0: also known as Cosbower, and joins me now. Hi, Skye. Welcome back to the program.
Speaker 0: Hi, Sally. It's good to be joining you. But before we discuss the legislative agenda, the Microsoft Outlook outage hit businesses across Australia
Speaker 0: on Friday.
Speaker 0: Does Kosboa have a sense of how much the technology failure may have cost small businesses?
Speaker 1: We know for small businesses, it takes a hit on productivity. Many small businesses will shut down for a whole day of operations,
Speaker 1: and particularly those businesses working in a more white collar sector
Speaker 1: have... Will really feel the impact of that. Many of them will be scrambling today to catch up as a result.
Speaker 0: Let's look at trusts. Your organization has written to senators along with four other major national business and industry organizations.
Speaker 0: You're urging senators not to pass the government's proposed discretionary
Speaker 0: tax...
Speaker 0: Trust tax changes in their current form. Why is that?
Speaker 1: So the announcement that was made in the budget was that the government would introduce a 30% minimum on discretionary trusts.
Speaker 1: I think a lot of us tend to think of discretionary trusts as particularly investment vehicles for wealthy Australians,
Speaker 1: but the reality is that there's about 350,000
Speaker 1: small family businesses. The vast majority of them, which are probably better described as micro family businesses,
Speaker 1: who are operating through discretionary trusts.
Speaker 1: And the bill as it is currently drafted gives those businesses three bad options,
Speaker 1: all of which will make it harder for them to do business.
Speaker 0: Last month, we spoke to Dale Bocabella,
Speaker 0: associate professor of tax law at the University of New South Wales. He says current arrangements allow for tax minimization. Let's take a listen. I'll just give you a couple of examples. Everybody knows a 17 year old
Speaker 2: with an Into Vivo's trust, a trust that's been created by a person who's alive,
Speaker 2: a 17 year old won't be getting much of an allocation because they'll be subject to the penalty rate. As soon as the person turns 18,
Speaker 2: guess what? They get $2,223,000.
Speaker 2: Why? Because that's essentially
Speaker 2: the tax free threshold. In this... So that's the way it's used to allocate the income
Speaker 2: to a beneficiary
Speaker 2: who has a very favorable tax profile.
Speaker 0: If profits are transferred to a person with a more favorable tax profile,
Speaker 0: how does this benefit the actual business
Speaker 0: itself?
Speaker 1: So what Dale's talking about there is something that we call income splitting,
Speaker 1: and I think it's important to recognize that we have said to the government, if they think income splitting is inappropriate,
Speaker 1: if they think that's problematic
Speaker 1: tax behavior,
Speaker 1: we are supportive of working with them to address that behavior.
Speaker 1: What we're doing here by introducing
Speaker 1: a 30% minimum tax on discretionary trust isn't targeting a per... Behavior that they think is problematic.
Speaker 1: It's making collateral damage of 350,000
Speaker 1: small family businesses
Speaker 1: by taking a very blunt instrument
Speaker 1: to address a very specific behavior.
Speaker 0: Would the government be able to amend its proposal to your satisfaction,
Speaker 0: or should it simply dump the idea
Speaker 0: of changing the tax arrangements for discretionary trusts?
Speaker 1: We would definitely prefer that they simply dump the idea altogether.
Speaker 1: As I said, we support integrity in the tax system, and we are very happy to work with the government on promoting integrity in the tax system. But targeted measures are the way to do that rather than the blunt measure that is on the table. If the government does go ahead with the bill as it's currently legislated,
Speaker 1: the options to remove or reduce some of the harm that is going to be be had on hundreds of thousands of small family businesses is to grandfather those businesses. So to essentially say,
Speaker 1: already as businesses already established in discretionary trust continue to operate with existing arrangements.
Speaker 0: You're listening to Radio National Breakfast. My guest is the CEO of COSBOA,
Speaker 0: Sky Kapuki. Sky, the government is trying to tweak its capital gains tax changes proposing a carve out for
Speaker 0: innovative startups. Does Kosboa see merit in the government's attempts to address the concerns of startup founders?
Speaker 1: So we were pleased that the government
Speaker 1: began this conversation and had the consultation about how they would reduce the impact of the of the harm of the changes to the capital gains tax discount
Speaker 1: on innovative businesses.
Speaker 1: I would say, however, that the IBCC,
Speaker 1: which is the concession that is currently on the table, is complex. It's hard for businesses to know ahead of time whether or not it's something that they will will be eligible for. AllegroSpender
Speaker 1: has put an alternative on the table, and we are urging the government to consider this closely.
Speaker 1: So it's an alternative
Speaker 1: that is is not as good as what we've currently got. It's not as good as the 50%
Speaker 1: discount
Speaker 1: that is currently in place and that enables supports and fosters business investment,
Speaker 1: but it is better than what the government is proposing that we move to. And LEGRA is saying that that we should be exploring instead of the IBCC
Speaker 1: as a cost neutral measure to the IBCC,
Speaker 1: a 40%
Speaker 1: capital gains tax discount for all business assets.
Speaker 0: Just finally, more broadly, all these proposed legislative changes come after the RBA hiked interest rates for a fifth time this year amid
Speaker 0: stubborn inflation. How much pressure are small businesses under right now?
Speaker 1: Sally,
Speaker 1: small businesses are are doing it tough. It's been a very challenging year, and it's felt like one hit after another. As you said, there's been five interest rate rises this year, had sustained periods of low consumer confidence.
Speaker 1: The small business sector has also had a number of policy decisions implemented that put pressure put pressure on cash flow,
Speaker 1: including the introduction of payday slew... Super, including the ban on the credit card surcharges,
Speaker 1: and small businesses across the country are telling us that the pressure is adding up. They are really feeling it.
Speaker 0: Skye Kapuka, thank you for joining me this morning. Thanks, Sally.
actors: Council of Small Business Organizations Australia (COSBOA)
themes: Government proposes 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts affecting 350,000 small family businesses
Microsoft Outlook outage causes significant productivity losses for Australian small businesses
Government capital gains tax changes with proposed carve-out for innovative startups faces criticism
Small businesses facing mounting pressure from five RBA interest rate rises and multiple policy changes
